title: First in my family to graduate
description: From late-night library sessions to walking across the stage in Leicester, this is a story about the community that cheered me on.
body: When I arrived in the UK at eighteen, I did not know anyone in my city. A ZOCF prayer call connected me with another Zambian student two streets away, and that friendship carried me through three years of exams.
Graduation day felt like a family celebration, even though most of my family were watching on a video call from Lusaka. Members I had only met a few times turned up with flowers and chitenge outfits.
My advice to anyone starting out: find your people early. You do not have to do it alone.

title: From my kitchen to a catering business
description: How cooking for church events turned into a small Zambian catering company, and what I learned about starting a business.
body: It started with cooking nshima and ifisashi for fellowship gatherings. People kept asking whether I could cater their parties.
I took a free business course, registered my company and found a mentor through the community. The first year was hard, but every event taught me something.
If you have an idea, start small and ask for help. Our community is full of people who want you to succeed.

title: Landing my first tech job
description: Fifty applications, three interviews and one yes. What helped me break into software engineering.
body: I switched from a maths degree to software engineering through evening courses and a lot of practice projects.
Mock interviews with other young professionals made the biggest difference. They told me honestly where I was going wrong.
Now I run a small coding club so others can get the same support.

title: Saturdays at the food bank
description: What started as a one-off volunteering day became a monthly tradition for a group of young members in Manchester.
body: Six of us signed up for one Saturday. Now there are fifteen of us, and the food bank team know us by name.
Serving together has built friendships faster than any social event. You learn a lot about someone while packing two hundred food parcels.
Anyone can join: no experience needed, just a willing heart.

title: Teaching traditional dance on Independence Day
description: Young members led the dance workshop at this year's Independence celebration, and the children did not want it to end.
body: Our grandmothers taught us these dances. This year we taught them to children born in the UK, Ireland and Canada.
Seeing kids in chitenge wraps learning moves from home was one of the proudest moments of my year.
Culture stays alive when we share it, and NextGen gives us the space to do that.

title: Our first NextGen hike in the Highlands
description: Eight people, one mountain and a lot of laughter. Why getting outdoors together matters.
body: Most of the group had never climbed a mountain. We took it slowly, shared snacks and stopped for plenty of photos.
At the top, someone started singing a Zambian worship song and everyone joined in. It is a memory I will keep for a long time.
Next time we are aiming for two mountains. Who is coming?
